entities.name: Chamber of States
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Chamber of States (Ständerat), Switzerland's upper chamber — part of the Federal Assembly alongside the National Council — is the council representing Switzerland's 26 cantons and half-cantons, with each full canton sending 2 representatives and each half-canton 1, regardless of population size. The 46-member chamber has co-equal legislative power with the National Council (200 seats based on population) and embodies Switzerland's federal principle that the Confederation is a union of equal sovereign states as well as a democratic state of equal citizens.

The Chamber of States (modeled partly on the US Senate) represents the cantonal dimension of Swiss federalism — a particularly important institution given that Switzerland's extreme decentralization gives cantons responsibility for education, health, police, and significant taxation. Swiss cantons range from Geneva (population 500,000) to Appenzell Innerrhoden (16,000), all sending equal delegates to the Ständerat.

The chamber's political dynamics are distinctive: because rural, smaller, and more conservative cantons are overrepresented relative to their population, the Chamber of States tends to lean more right and centrist than the population-based National Council. The Swiss People's Party (SVP/UDC) — which wins the most seats in the National Council — tends to underperform in the Ständerat because its support is concentrated in populous cantons. The two chambers must agree on all legislation; when they disagree, a conference committee resolves differences. The chamber has served since 1848 as one of the world's most enduring federal upper houses.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Switzerland's Chamber of States — the equal-cantonal-representation upper house operating since 1848, moderating Swiss federal legislation through bicameral requirement, and embodying the world's most extreme federalism — is one of the most stable and sophisticated federal legislative chambers in history.
